intro.title: Your first R code
intro.bodyMarkdown:
R is a programming language made for working with data. Scientists, analysts, journalists and students use it to tidy data, summarise it, run statistics and make charts. In CodeQuest, R runs right here in your browser: type code, press **Run**, and the result appears underneath.

The simplest R code is a calculation. R works it out and shows the answer:

```
2 + 3
10 * 4
```

R shows `[1] 5` and `[1] 40`. The `[1]` is not part of the answer: it means "this line starts with the first value". Later you will meet results with many values, where it helps you count them. For now, read `[1] 5` as "the answer is 5".

To show text, put it in quotes and give it to `print()`. R shows text with its quotes, so you can tell it is text:

```
print("Hello, R!")
```

That shows `[1] "Hello, R!"`. When you want just the words, without the `[1]` and the quotes, use `cat()`. `cat()` doesn't start a new line by itself, so end the text with `\n`, which means "new line":

```
cat("Hello, R!\n")
```

`cat()` can show several things at once, separated by commas. It puts a space between them, and it works out any maths first: `cat("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3, "\n")` shows `2 + 3 = 5`.

A line that starts with `#` is a **comment**. R skips it: comments are notes for people reading your code. A comment can also go at the end of a line.

```
# the number of days in a year
365  # not a leap year
```

R is **case-sensitive**: `print` works, but `Print` gives the error `could not find function "Print"`. Every challenge checks the result of your code, so read errors carefully, fix the line, and run it again.

intro.title: Doing the maths
intro.bodyMarkdown:
R is a very good calculator. These are the arithmetic operators:

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | add | `7 + 2` | `9` |
| `-` | subtract | `7 - 2` | `5` |
| `*` | multiply | `7 * 2` | `14` |
| `/` | divide | `7 / 2` | `3.5` |
| `^` | to the power of | `7 ^ 2` | `49` |
| `%/%` | whole-number division | `7 %/% 2` | `3` |
| `%%` | remainder | `7 %% 2` | `1` |

Division gives decimals when it needs to: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. Decimals use a point, never a comma.

Whole-number division and remainder go together. 50 eggs fill `50 %/% 6`, that is 8, boxes of six, with `50 %% 6`, that is 2, eggs left over. The remainder is also how you test for even numbers: an even number has remainder 0 when divided by 2.

R follows the usual order of operations: powers first, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`. Use brackets to change the order, just like on paper:

```
2 + 3 * 4    # 14: multiply first
(2 + 3) * 4  # 20: brackets first
```

Spaces around operators are optional, but they make code easier to read. R shows very big and very small numbers in **scientific notation**: `1e6` means 1 followed by 6 zeros, a million, and `2.5e-3` is 0.0025. You can type numbers that way too.

When you run several lines, R shows the result of each one in turn:

```
12 * 3
200 %/% 60
200 %% 60
```

questions.explanation: Multiplication comes before addition: 3 × 4 is 12, plus 2 is 14.
Brackets go first: 2 + 3 is 5, times 4 is 20.
`^` is "to the power of": 2 × 2 × 2 is 8.
`%%` gives the remainder: 17 is 3 fives (15) with 2 left over.
`%/%` is whole-number division: 5 goes into 17 three whole times.
`/` is ordinary division and keeps the decimals.

`e3` means "times 10 to the power 3", so 2e3 is 2 × 1000 = 2000.
An even number has no remainder when divided by 2.

intro.title: Saving values with <-
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **variable** is a name for a value, so you can use it again later. You make one with the arrow `<-`, read as "gets": `cups <- 3` means "`cups` gets 3".

```
cups <- 3
price <- 2.5
cups * price
```

Saving a value shows nothing. To see a variable, type its name on its own line, or `print()` it. The last line above shows `[1] 7.5`, worked out from the two variables.

Variables can hold text too: `city <- "Lisbon"`. Text always needs quotes; a name without quotes is a variable.

You can give a variable a new value at any time, even one worked out from its old value. This adds 1 to `score`:

```
score <- 10
score <- score + 1
score
```

A variable keeps the value it was given. If you change `price` later, a total you worked out earlier stays the same until you work it out again.

Names can use letters, numbers, `.` and `_`, but can't start with a number and can't contain spaces or `-`. Good names say what the value is: `total_price`, `n_guests`. R is case-sensitive, so `total` and `Total` are two different names.

You may also see `=` used to save values (`cups = 3`). It works, but `<-` is the usual R style, and it's what this course uses. A handy trick: wrap an assignment in brackets to save the value and show it at once: `(cups <- 3)`.

cups <- 3
price <- 2.5
cups * price
total <- cups * price
total

intro.title: Working with text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Text in R is called a **string** (R also calls it "character"). It goes in double quotes `"..."` or single quotes `'...'`; both work the same. Use single quotes around text that contains double quotes: `'She said "hi"'`.

`paste()` joins pieces of text, with a space between them. `paste0()` joins them with nothing in between. Numbers are turned into text along the way:

```
paste("Good", "morning")   # "Good morning"
paste0("bike", 42)          # "bike42"
paste("Table", 4, "of", 12) # "Table 4 of 12"
```

To join with something else, give `paste()` a `sep` (separator): `paste("2026", "10", "30", sep = "-")` gives `"2026-10-30"`.

A few functions for working with text:

| Function | What it does | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nchar()` | counts the characters | `nchar("garden")` | `6` |
| `toupper()` | capital letters | `toupper("open")` | `"OPEN"` |
| `tolower()` | small letters | `tolower("SALE")` | `"sale"` |

`nchar()` counts every character, spaces included: `nchar("R is fun")` is 8.

Text that looks like a number is still text. `"5" + 1` gives an error, because R can't add text. Leave the quotes off numbers you want to calculate with.

To show a finished message, `cat()` is usually best: it shows the words without quotes, and puts a space between the pieces, like `paste()`.

```
name <- "Ana"
greeting <- paste("Hello,", name)
cat(greeting, "\n")
```

greeting <- paste("Hello,", name)
greeting
cat(greeting, "\n")
nchar(greeting)
toupper(greeting)

intro.title: TRUE and FALSE
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A comparison asks R a yes-or-no question, and the answer is `TRUE` or `FALSE`. These are **logical** values, written in capitals and without quotes.

| Operator | Question | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `==` | equal? | `3 == 3` | `TRUE` |
| `!=` | not equal? | `3 != 3` | `FALSE` |
| `<` | less than? | `2 < 5` | `TRUE` |
| `>` | greater than? | `2 > 5` | `FALSE` |
| `<=` | less than or equal? | `5 <= 5` | `TRUE` |
| `>=` | greater than or equal? | `4 >= 5` | `FALSE` |

Equality is a **double** `==`. A single `=` saves a value (like `<-`), so `x = 5` changes `x`, while `x == 5` asks whether `x` is 5.

Text can be compared too. `"tea" == "tea"` is `TRUE`, but `"Tea" == "tea"` is `FALSE`: capitals count.

Combine questions with `&` (and: both must be true) and `|` (or: at least one must be true). `!` (not) turns `TRUE` into `FALSE` and back.

```
temperature <- 24
sunny <- TRUE
temperature > 20 & sunny   # TRUE: both are true
temperature > 30 | sunny   # TRUE: one is enough
!sunny                     # FALSE
```

Logical values can be saved in variables like any other value, and later stages use them to choose rows of data and decide what code runs. One more trick: in arithmetic, `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, so `TRUE + TRUE` is 2. That makes counting easy, as you will see with vectors.

intro.title: Calling functions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **function** does a job for you. You call it by name, with its inputs, called **arguments**, in brackets. You have already used `print()`, `cat()`, `paste()` and `nchar()`. R has thousands more; here are some for numbers:

| Function | What it does | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sqrt()` | square root | `sqrt(144)` | `12` |
| `abs()` | drops the minus sign | `abs(-7)` | `7` |
| `round()` | rounds | `round(3.14159, 2)` | `3.14` |
| `ceiling()` | rounds up | `ceiling(4.2)` | `5` |
| `floor()` | rounds down | `floor(4.8)` | `4` |
| `max()`, `min()` | largest, smallest | `max(18, 42, 27)` | `42` |

Some functions take several arguments, separated by commas. `round(3.14159, 2)` rounds to 2 decimal places. Arguments have names, and you can write them out, which makes code easier to read: `round(3.14159, digits = 2)` does the same thing. Named arguments can go in any order.

Leave out an argument that has a default, and R uses the default: `round(3.7)` rounds to a whole number, 4.

One surprise: R rounds a 5 to the nearest **even** number, so `round(2.5)` is 2 and `round(3.5)` is 4. Statisticians do this so rounding doesn't push totals up on average.

You can put one function call inside another. R works from the inside out:

```
round(sqrt(50), 1)   # sqrt first: 7.071..., then round: 7.1
```

To read about any function, type `?` and its name, such as `?round`, in RStudio or the R console. The help pages list every argument and its default. (Help pages don't open inside CodeQuest; the **Read more** link at the end of each stage points to R's manuals.)

intro.title: Missing values: NA
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real data has gaps: a survey question someone skipped, a day the sensor was off, a price nobody wrote down. R marks a missing value with `NA`, short for "not available". It is written without quotes.

```
rating <- NA
rating
```

R is careful with `NA`. If a value is unknown, anything worked out from it is unknown too, so maths with `NA` gives `NA`:

```
NA + 1      # NA
NA * 0      # NA
NA > 5      # NA
```

Even `NA == NA` is `NA`: two unknown values might or might not be the same. So you can't test for a missing value with `==`. Use `is.na()`, which gives `TRUE` or `FALSE`:

```
is.na(rating)   # TRUE
is.na(42)       # FALSE
!is.na(42)      # TRUE: it has a value
```

Sometimes R can answer even with a gap. `TRUE | NA` is `TRUE`, because "true or anything" is true. `FALSE & NA` is `FALSE`, because "false and anything" is false.

Watch out for the text `"NA"` in quotes. That is two letters, not a missing value: `is.na("NA")` is `FALSE`. Data files sometimes contain it by mistake, and a later quest shows how to clean it up.

Once you have many values, R lets you skip the `NA`s when you add them up or take an average. That's in the next quest, Vectors.

intro.title: Reading error messages
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Everyone who writes code makes mistakes, all the time. The skill is reading what R tells you and fixing it quickly. When R can't run a line, it stops and shows an **error**. Nothing after that line runs.

These are the errors you will meet most often:

| Error | Usual cause | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `object 'totl' not found` | a misspelt variable, or one not made yet | `totl * 2` |
| `could not find function "sqroot"` | a misspelt function name | `sqroot(16)` |
| `unexpected end of input` | a bracket or quote never closed | `round(3.456, 1` |
| `unexpected numeric constant` | a missing comma or operator | `max(3 8)` |
| `unexpected string constant` | a missing comma before some text | `paste("a" "b")` |
| `non-numeric argument to binary operator` | maths on text | `"12" * 2` |

The message usually names the problem word. `object 'totl' not found` points straight at `totl`. For "unexpected" errors, R shows the line with a `^` under the spot where it got confused: look just before it.

A **warning** is different from an error. R still runs the line and gives an answer, but tells you something looks wrong. `sqrt(-4)` gives `NaN` ("not a number") with a warning, because negative numbers have no ordinary square root.

A good routine: read the error, find the line, fix one thing, and run again. When there are several mistakes, R stops at the first, so fix them one at a time.

```
# Run this, read the error, and fix the typo
total <- 12
totl * 2
```
intro.sandboxCode:
# Run this, read the error, then fix it
total <- 12
totl * 2

intro.title: Easy side quest: The café bill
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Corner Café sells lattes for 3.40 and croissants for 2.80. A table orders **two lattes and one croissant**, adds a 10% tip, and splits the bill three ways.

Build the bill step by step, saving each result in a variable. The last challenge puts it all together and shows the bill:

```
Subtotal: 9.6
Tip: 0.96
Total: 10.56
Each pays: 3.52
```

Round money to 2 decimal places with `round(x, 2)`. Note that `cat()` shows `9.6`, not `9.60`: R drops zeros at the end of a number. A later quest shows how to format money with two decimals.

```

```

latte <- 3.4
croissant <- 2.8

Two decimal places: 0.964 is nearer 0.96.

intro.title: Medium side quest: A bike-share ride
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Riverside Bikes charges **1.00 to unlock** a bike, plus **0.15 per minute**. A rider unlocks a bike at 8:12 and returns it at 8:59, after riding 9.4 km.

Times are easiest to work with as minutes since midnight: 8:12 is `8 * 60 + 12`, which is 492, and 8:59 is 539.

Work out the ride step by step. The last challenge shows a summary:

```
Ride: 47 min, 9.4 km
Speed: 12 km/h
Cost: 8.05
Long ride: TRUE
```

challenges.title: Easy: Minutes since midnight
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `start` the minutes since midnight at 8:12, and `end` at 8:59. Let R work them out from the hours and minutes.

challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `minutes` the length of the ride.

challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `cost` the price of the ride: 1.00 to unlock plus 0.15 per minute.

challenges.title: Medium: The speed
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `speed` the average speed in km per hour, rounded to 1 decimal place. Speed is distance divided by time in **hours**.
challenges.hint: The time in hours is `minutes / 60`: `speed <- round(km / (minutes / 60), 1)`.

challenges.title: Hard: A long ride?
challenges.promptMarkdown: Rides over 45 minutes count as long. Make `long_ride` TRUE or FALSE for this ride.

challenges.title: Expert: The ride summary
challenges.promptMarkdown:
From the start and end times and the distance, work everything out and show:

```
Ride: 47 min, 9.4 km
Speed: 12 km/h
Cost: 8.05
Long ride: TRUE
```
challenges.hint: Work out `minutes`, `speed`, `cost` and `long_ride`, then use `cat()` for each line. For the first line, `cat()` puts a space before the comma unless the comma is part of the text: `cat("Ride:", minutes, "min,", km, "km\n")`.
challenges.solution:
start <- 8 * 60 + 12
end <- 8 * 60 + 59
km <- 9.4
minutes <- end - start
speed <- round(km / (minutes / 60), 1)
cost <- 1 + 0.15 * minutes
long_ride <- minutes > 45
cat("Ride:", minutes, "min,", km, "km\n")
cat("Speed:", speed, "km/h\n")
cat("Cost:", cost, "\n")
cat("Long ride:", long_ride, "\n")

tests.label: Shows the summary
tests.assertion: identical(trimws(strsplit(._cq_stdout, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "right"), c("Ride: 47 min, 9.4 km", "Speed: 12 km/h", "Cost: 8.05", "Long ride: TRUE"))

Multiply first: 7.05, plus 1 is 8.05.

intro.title: Hard side quest: The garden harvest
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Five families share the Elm Street community garden. At the end of the season they weigh the harvest: **12.4 kg of tomatoes** and **8.75 kg of courgettes**. Nobody weighed the beans on the day, so for now the beans are missing.

Later someone finds the note: the beans weighed **3.6 kg**. Then the families share the harvest equally and write a short report:

```
Harvest: 24.75 kg
Per family: 4.95 kg
More tomatoes than courgettes: TRUE
Top crop: TOMATOES
```

This side quest uses everything in the quest: variables, arithmetic, `NA`, comparisons, functions and text.

beans <- NA
courgettes <- 8.75
tomatoes + beans + courgettes

challenges.solution:

challenges.title: Expert: The harvest report
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Starting from the weights, show the report:

```
Harvest: 24.75 kg
Per family: 4.95 kg
More tomatoes than courgettes: TRUE
Top crop: TOMATOES
```

Make `top_crop` the text `"tomatoes"` in capitals with `toupper()`.
challenges.hint: Work out `total`, `share` and `more_tomatoes` as before, set `top_crop <- toupper("tomatoes")`, then four `cat()` lines. The first is `cat("Harvest:", total, "kg\n")`.
challenges.solution:
tomatoes <- 12.4
courgettes <- 8.75
beans <- 3.6
families <- 5
total <- tomatoes + beans + courgettes
share <- round(total / families, 2)
more_tomatoes <- tomatoes > courgettes
top_crop <- toupper("tomatoes")
cat("Harvest:", total, "kg\n")
cat("Per family:", share, "kg\n")
cat("More tomatoes than courgettes:", more_tomatoes, "\n")
cat("Top crop:", top_crop, "\n")

tests.label: Shows the report
tests.assertion: identical(trimws(strsplit(._cq_stdout, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "right"), c("Harvest: 24.75 kg", "Per family: 4.95 kg", "More tomatoes than courgettes: TRUE", "Top crop: TOMATOES"))

questions.explanation: One unknown weight makes the total unknown.
3.6 is a real value, so it is not missing.
24.75 / 5 is exactly 4.95.
`toupper()` gives text, so R shows it in quotes, all in capitals.
12.4 is greater than 8.75.

questions.explanation: `NA` (no quotes) means "not available".
